title: Isolated Solve-Then-Judge: A Simple Defense Against Candidate-Response Prompt Injection for Multimodal LLM Judges

contributions.purpose: Defend multimodal LLM judges against prompt injection attacks embedded in candidate responses.
contributions.mechanism: A two-pass architecture where Pass 1 generates a self-answer from only trusted inputs (image + query) and Pass 2 judges candidates against this uncontaminated reference.
contributions.evaluation: Evaluated on VL-RewardBench (N=1,247) with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, reducing conditional attack success rate from 91.3% to 29.3%.
contributions.source_quote: A two-pass architecture where Pass 1 generates a self-answer from only trusted inputs (image + query), and Pass 2 judges candidates against this uncontaminated reference.

contributions.purpose: Quantify the defense's effectiveness and isolate what causes it.
contributions.mechanism: Empirical evaluation on VL-RewardBench with controlled experiments separating information isolation from prompt engineering effects.
contributions.evaluation: 62 percentage-point reduction in conditional attack success rate (from 91.3% to 29.3%), with information isolation contributing an additional 4pp defense beyond prompt engineering alone.
contributions.source_quote: Empirical evaluation demonstrating a 62 percentage-point reduction in conditional attack success rate (from 91.3% to 29.3%), with controlled experiments isolating the contribution of information isolation versus prompt engineering.

contributions.purpose: Characterize the costs and limits of the defense across attack categories.
contributions.mechanism: Trade-off and per-category analysis of clean accuracy degradation and residual attack success.
contributions.evaluation: 10.8pp clean accuracy cost; strongest for hallucination detection (74.8pp reduction), weakest for reasoning tasks (36.4pp); authority impersonation attacks still achieve 63.6% success.
contributions.source_quote: Analysis of trade-offs (10.8pp accuracy cost), category-dependent effectiveness (strongest for hallucination detection, weakest for reasoning), and remaining vulnerabilities (authority impersonation attacks achieve 63.6% success).

self_declared_provenance.quote: Lin et al. (2025) proposed self-reference-guided evaluation, demonstrating that leveraging a judge model's own response as a reference strengthens the correlation between generation and judgment capabilities. These defenses have not been specifically evaluated for LLM-as-a-Judge scenarios where adversarial content is embedded in candidate responses.

notes: Paper explicitly reports significant costs and residual vulnerabilities: 10.8pp clean accuracy degradation and 63.6% attack success for authority impersonation even under defense (partial negative results acknowledged in abstract).
